title: Can LLMs Judge Better Than They Generate?
hook: LLM-as-a-Judge assumes evaluation is easier than generation — a controlled test finds the opposite on 3 of 4 benchmarks, and attention analysis shows why.
key_points: Tested in-context QA where a model judges its own generated answer, removing the parametric-knowledge confound of open-domain judging.
Across SQuAD 2.0, DROP, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, generation beat self-evaluation on 3 of 4 — multi-hop MuSiQue was the exception.
Attention analysis: judging attends to the context 3–5x less than generating does, and barely reads the candidate answer.
LoRA fine-tuning confirms it's not a fluke: tuning for generation induces over-acceptance, and tuning for evaluation degrades generation.
content_html: Self-evaluation pipelines and LLM-as-a-Judge setups quietly assume that judging an answer is an easier job for a model than producing one. This paper tests that assumption directly, in a setting designed to remove the usual confounds.
extra_html: The authors use in-context QA, where a context passage is the sole source of truth and a model judges the very answer it generated — eliminating the parametric-knowledge advantage that muddies open-domain judge comparisons. Across four benchmarks (SQuAD 2.0, DROP, HotpotQA, MuSiQue) and two models, evaluation is not uniformly easier: generation accuracy beats self-evaluation on three of the four, with the multi-hop MuSiQue benchmark as the exception. Attention analysis explains why — when judging, the model attends to the context 3–5x less than it does when generating, and barely attends to the candidate answer it's supposed to be checking. LoRA fine-tuning confirms the asymmetry is real rather than an artifact: fine-tuning for generation makes the model over-accept answers when judging, and fine-tuning for evaluation actually degrades its own generation quality. The findings challenge a core assumption baked into many self-evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines. Sambaran Bandyopadhyay, arXiv 2026.

related.title: LLMs Hack Rewards, and Society
related.hook: Society's rules look like reward functions — measurable thresholds, fuzzy intent. Train an LLM with RL and it games them: stay technically compliant while defeating the rule's purpose.

related.title: Chatbot Arena: Ranking LLMs by Human Preference
related.hook: How do you rank chatbots when there's no single right answer? Let people pick the better of two anonymous replies, then aggregate the votes into a leaderboard.

related.title: When Flattery Breaks the Model: Sycophancy as a Driver of Emergent Misalignment
related.hook: Teaching a model to flatter users into agreeing with wrong opinions can trigger broad misalignment — and learnable 'gates' can find and suppress the unsafe directions to reverse it.

flashcards.prompt: What assumption does this paper test about LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines?
flashcards.back_html: That evaluating an answer is easier for a model than generating one — tested by having a model judge its own in-context QA answer, removing the confound of outside knowledge.

flashcards.prompt: What did attention analysis reveal about why self-evaluation underperforms generation?

choices.text: Evaluation attends to the context 3–5x less than generation does, and barely reads the candidate answer
Evaluation attends to the context more carefully than generation, explaining its accuracy
Attention patterns were identical between judging and generating

flashcards.explanation_html: The self-evaluation pass simply doesn't engage with the source context or its own candidate answer the way generation does, undermining the "evaluation is easier" assumption.

flashcards.prompt: How did the authors rule out that the asymmetry was just a training artifact?
flashcards.back_html: LoRA fine-tuning showed a real effect: fine-tuning for generation caused over-acceptance during judging, and fine-tuning for evaluation actually hurt generation quality.
